extracted.intended_audience: judge advocates, military lawyers, court-martial members, and practitioners of military justice
extracted.subtask_description: Authoritative interpretive rules and procedural guidance under the Articles of War governing court-martial practice (e.g., challenges, depositions, continuances, punishments, double jeopardy, sentencing, and admissibility of depositions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reopening court to receive previous convictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Held that the reopening of the court, after a conviction, to receive evidence of previous convictions, was not a violation of the eighty-fourth article of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure accords with spirit of legislation excluding judge advocates from closed sessions — allows the accused to be present when evidence of previous convictions is submitted and to scrutinize and test the legality of the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of finding to clerk during deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosing of the finding and sentence to a clerk by permitting him to remain with the court at the final deliberation and enter the judgment in the record is a violation of the oath and a grave irregularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a grave irregularity, such disclosure does not affect the validity of the proceedings or sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of power to punish under contempt article
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of a court-martial to punish, under this article, being confined practically to acts done in its immediate presence, such a court can have no authority to punish a neglect by an officer or soldier to attend as a witness in compliance with a summons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punitive power is limited to contempts committed in the court's immediate presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluding disorderly persons from sessions
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial is authorized to exclude from its session any person who it has good reason to believe will endeavor to intimidate or interrupt the witnesses, or otherwise conduct himself in a disorderly manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court may preserve order by excluding potential interrupters or intimidators.

rubrics_metrics.name: No common-law contempt power; civilian witness refusal
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial has none of the common-law power to punish for contempt vested in the ordinary courts of justice, but only such authority as is given it by this article; thus a court-martial was not authorized to punish, as for a contempt, a civilian witness duly summoned and appearing before it, but, when put on the stand, declining (without disorder) to testify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts-martial must look to statutory authority for contempt powers; civilians refusing to testify cannot be punished by the court-martial as contempt under this authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure when contempt by military person occurs
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contempt within the description of this article has been committed, and the court deems it proper that the offender shall be punished, the proper course is to suspend the regular business, and after giving the party an opportunity to be heard, explain, etc., to proceed — if the explanation is insufficient — to impose a punishment; resuming thereupon the original proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Action is properly summary (no formal trial). Usual punishments: close confinement in quarters or guardhouse during trial of pending case, or forfeiture of a reasonable amount of pay. Alternative: bring the person to trial before a new court on a charge for a disorder under art. 62.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge advocate process authority not vesting contempt power
rubrics_metrics.description: The authority of the judge advocate to issue like process to compel witnesses to appear and testify which courts of criminal jurisdiction within the State, Territory, or district where such military courts may be ordered to sit, may lawfully issue, does not vest the court-martial with power to punish a civilian witness for contempt who refuses to testify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power to procure process does not carry with it contempt-punishment authority over civilians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient grounds to challenge a court member
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficient grounds of challenge to a member include: that the member is the author of the charges and a material witness in the case; that he is the prosecutor in the case; that he had expressed an opinion based upon the knowledge of the facts that the accused would be convicted whichever way he might plead; that a member was present at a mutiny related to the charge; that he said he would not associate with the accused; that he had previously investigated the case as a member of a board of survey, court of inquiry, or a previous court-martial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cited decisions illustrate factual situations that justify excusing a member for bias or direct involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficient grounds to excuse a court member
rubrics_metrics.description: A member should not be excused on challenge for: mere fact he is to be a witness; that he ministerially or by order of a superior preferred the charges; that he was in command of the accused; that he is junior to the accused (unless promotion would result from dismissal); that he entertained an opinion as to the impropriety of acts charged unaccompanied by any opinion as to guilt; or that he had a disagreement with the accused while declaring no prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories are generally not enough, standing alone, to establish disqualifying bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing to raise challenge objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Where before arraignment the accused, without having personal knowledge of the existence of a ground of challenge to a member, had credible information of its existence, he should properly have raised the objection before the members were sworn, and the court is not in error in refusing to allow him to take it at a subsequent stage of the trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenges should be made promptly — typically before members are sworn — when the accused has (or should have) knowledge or credible information of grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court as a whole not subject to challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: The court, as a whole, is not subject to challenge; yet all the members may be challenged provided they are challenged separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass challenge is not permitted; individual challenges must be made against each member.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of depositions for high-ranking witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the evidence of high officers or public officials is required before a court-martial, the same, especially if the court is assembled at a distant point, should be taken by deposition, if authorized under this article; such officers should not be required to leave their public duties to attend as witnesses, except where their depositions will not be admissible, and where the case is one of special importance and their testimony is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary of War and other high officials generally should not be required to attend; use depositions when practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must offer entire deposition or none
rubrics_metrics.description: The party at whose instance a deposition has been taken should not be permitted to introduce only such parts of the deposition as are favorable to him or as he may elect to use; he must offer the deposition in evidence as a whole or not offer it at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial use of deposition to the exclusion of other parts is prohibited — fairness requires offering the whole deposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other party may read deposition if instigator declines to use it
rubrics_metrics.description: If the party at whose instance a deposition has been taken decides not to put it in, it may be read in evidence by the other party. One party cannot withhold a deposition (duly taken and admissible under this article) without the consent of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents tactical withholding of depositions; either admit whole deposition or permit adversary to use it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-country depositions procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: When it is necessary to take a deposition in a foreign country, the papers should be forwarded to The Adjutant General for submission to the Department of State, with a request that a proper official of the diplomatic or consular service be designated to cause the deposition to be taken at the residence of the deponent or at the nearest point to such residence as is convenient for the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow diplomatic channels to procure properly administered foreign depositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may not refuse legal material deposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the ninety-first article of war a court may not decide that a legal and material deposition shall not be taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the deposition is legal and material, the court cannot bar its taking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentication required for deposition admissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A deposition introduced by either party which is not 'duly authenticated' should not be admitted in evidence by the court, although the other party may not object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depositions failing to show authority of the officer taking it or qualification to administer the oath are irregular and inadmissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-martial cannot authorize others to take depositions
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial has no power to qualify or authorize a commanding officer, or any other officer or person, to take a deposition or administer an oath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only proper civil or diplomatic authority may be used for qualifying persons to take depositions or administer oaths; the court itself lacks that power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sixth Amendment confrontation clause not applicable to courts-martial
rubrics_metrics.description: Article VI of the amendments declares that the accused shall be entitled 'to be confronted with the witnesses against him.' Held that this applies only to cases before the United States courts and not to accused persons before courts-martial, as courts-martial are not a part of the judiciary of the United States, but simply instrumentalities of the executive power. Therefore, where the offense is not capital a deposition may be introduced before a court-martial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confrontation rights as interpreted for federal courts do not automatically bar depositions in non-capital courts-martial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depositions inadmissible in capital cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A deposition cannot be read in evidence in a capital case, that is, in a case where the offense may be punished capitally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where death may be a punishment, depositions are not admissible as a substitute for live testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depositions of local-resident witnesses require consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The deposition of a witness who resides in a State, etc., within which the court is held, is not admissible except by consent of the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local witnesses should ordinarily testify in person unless both sides agree to deposition use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuance to obtain counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: It is in general good ground for a reasonable continuance that the accused needs time to procure the assistance of counsel, if it is made to appear that such counsel can probably be obtained within the time asked, and that the accused is not chargeable with remissness in not having already provided himself with counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should grant reasonable continuances to secure counsel when prospect of obtaining counsel is shown and delay not caused by accused's negligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuance when charges differ materially from served copy
rubrics_metrics.description: That the charges and specifications upon which an accused is arraigned differ in a material particular from those contained in the copy served upon him before arraignment, may well constitute a sufficient ground for granting him additional time for the preparation of his defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material variance between served charges and arraignment copy justifies extra preparation time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Death sentence validity when multiple offenses include a capital one
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence of death imposed by a court-martial, upon a conviction of several distinct offenses, will be authorized and legal if any one of such offenses is made capably punishable by the Articles of War, although the other offenses may not be so punishable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any convicted offense is capital, death sentence may be lawfully imposed based on that offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court should not designate time or place of execution
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial, in imposing a death sentence, should not designate a time or place for its execution, such a designation not being within its province but pertaining to that of the reviewing authority; if it does so designate, this part of the sentence may be disregarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Execution logistics are for the reviewing authority, not the sentencing court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on penitentiary confinement for purely military offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: This article, by necessary implication, prohibits the imposition of confinement in a penitentiary as a punishment for offenses of a purely or exclusively military character — such as desertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purely military offenses should not be punished by civil penitentiary confinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penitentiary confinement allowed when offense is civil-equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: An offense duly charged as 'Conduct to the prejudice of good order and military discipline,' or as a violation of the sixtieth article of war, which, however, is in fact a larceny, embezzlement, violent crime, or other offense made punishable with penitentiary confinement by the law of the State, etc., may legally be visited with this punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the military charge in substance is a civil crime punishable by penitentiary, confinement in penitentiary may be imposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'penitentiary' in Article
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'penitentiary,' as employed in this article, has reference to civil prisons only — as the penitentiary of the United States or District of Columbia, the public prisons or penitentiaries of the different States, and the penitentiaries 'erected by the United States' in most of the Territories. The term State or State's prison in a sentence is equivalent to penitentiary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that 'penitentiary' refers to civil institutions rather than military prisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court discretion on term of penitentiary confinement
rubrics_metrics.description: A court-martial, in imposing by its sentence the punishment of confinement in a penitentiary, is not required to follow the statute of the United States or of the State, etc., as to the term of the confinement. It may adjudge, at its discretion, except as provided in the fifty-eighth article of war, a less or a greater term than that affixed by such statute to the particular offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not bound by civil statute terms, the court should often consult the statute as indicating a reasonable measure of punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation of place of confinement when multiple offenses involved
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier is convicted of manslaughter in violation of the sixty-second article of war, and shooting his superior officer in violation of the twenty-first article of war, and sentenced to imprisonment for life, held that as the maximum sentence for manslaughter in the State where the offense was committed is imprisonment in the penitentiary for eight years, the life imprisonment must be regarded as having been imposed under the twenty-first article of war, which defines a strictly military offense, so that under the ninety-seventh article of war the United States military prison, and not the United States Penitentiary, must be designated as the place of confinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sentence could derive from distinct civil and military offenses with different maximums, the character of the particular offense controlling the imposed punishment dictates whether military or civil prison is designated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'cowardice' and 'fraud' in Article
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms 'cowardice' and 'fraud,' employed in this article, may be considered as referring mainly to the offenses made punishable by articles 42 and 60; with these may be regarded as included all offenses in which fraud or cowardice is necessarily involved, though the same be not expressed in terms in the charge or specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broader interpretation includes offenses necessarily involving those characteristics even if not named.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity requirement compliance by Associated Press
rubrics_metrics.description: The publication throughout the United States, in the Associated Press dispatches, of the 'crime, punishment, name, and place of abode' of the accused, held to be a sufficient compliance with the requirements of the one hundredth article of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nationwide press dispatches can satisfy statutory publication/notification requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double jeopardy — 'tried' meaning and bar to second military trial
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution declares that 'no person shall be subjected, for the same offence, to be twice put in jeopardy of life or limb.' United States courts hold that 'tried' means duly prosecuted before a court-martial to a final conviction or acquittal; therefore, an officer or soldier, after having been duly convicted or acquitted by such a court, could not be subjected to a second military trial for the same offense, except by and upon his own waiver and consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finality of a court-martial conviction or acquittal bars re-prosecution for same offense absent waiver; decisions cited support the principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finality regardless of reviewing authority action
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the accused has been once duly convicted or acquitted, he has been 'tried' in the sense of the article, and cannot be tried again, against his will, though no action whatever be taken upon the proceedings by the reviewing authority; or though the proceedings, findings (and sentence, if any) be wholly disapproved by him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether or not the reviewing authority approves or acts upon the court-martial proceedings does not negate double-jeopardy protection once conviction/acquittal is final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions where no 'second' trial occurs
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no 'second' trial in cases where: the party after arraignment or trial before a court illegally constituted or without jurisdiction is again brought before a competent tribunal; where charges were substituted or withdrawn and new ones substituted before finality; where proceedings were discontinued without a finding and retried; where earlier court was dissolved or mistrial occurred at any stage before final acquittal/conviction; or where a previous trial was not a proper 'trial' (e.g., court not sworn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerates factual circumstances (mistrial, dissolution, lack of jurisdiction) in which re-trial is permissible and not barred by double jeopardy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent civil and military jurisdiction permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: It is no objection to the assuming by a court-martial of jurisdiction of a military offense that he may be amenable to trial, or may actually have been tried and convicted, by a criminal court of the State, etc., for a criminal offense involved in his act; a soldier may be tried by court-martial for a violation of article 21 after having been convicted by a State court for the criminal assault and battery, and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The same act may subject the offender to both jurisdictions; the act can be an offense against two jurisdictions and result in separate prosecutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil acquittal not necessarily a bar to later military trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an officer who had killed a superior officer in an altercation at a military post was brought to trial before a civil court on a charge of murder and acquitted, and was subsequently arraigned before a court-martial for an offense against military discipline involved in his criminal act, a plea of former trial was properly overruled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil acquittal does not automatically preclude military prosecution for distinct military offenses arising out of the same act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration of findings not a second trial
rubrics_metrics.description: The reconsideration by a court-martial of a finding, whether of guilty or not guilty, when duly reconvened for that purpose, is not a second trial within the meaning of this article; the original and revised proceedings are merely parts of one and the same trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reconvening to revise findings is treated as continuation of the same trial, not a new jeopardy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court of inquiry opinion not a former trial
rubrics_metrics.description: An opinion given by a court of inquiry is not in the nature of a sentence or adjudication pronounced upon a trial. The accused, upon a subsequent trial by court-martial of charges investigated by a court of inquiry, cannot plead the proceedings or opinion of the latter as a former trial, acquittal, or conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceedings and opinions of investigatory bodies do not have the finality of a trial judgment for double-jeopardy purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferencing military jurisdiction in sentinel/special-duty killings
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier on duty as sentinel at a military reservation commits homicide to prevent prisoners from escaping or in self-defense in the discharge of his duty, it is to the advantage of both military service and the soldier that he first be tried by a military court; to attain this, military jurisdiction should vest before the civil courts have assumed jurisdiction, and charges should be immediately formulated and lodged with proper authority to vest military jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance to secure military jurisdiction quickly in cases where the act arose from military duty.
